hud-bench-done: Komet HUD: benchmark done, results copied to clipboard and client log

verify-mismatch: The installed file does NOT match the checksum published for release {0}.
verify-norelease: GitHub has no release {0}, nothing to compare with.
verify-nofile: Loaded from a folder, there is no file to hash.
hud-spikes: Spikes over {0} ms or {1}× average, by cause
hud-spike-line: {0} s: {1} ms, {2} | GC {3} ms, between frames {4} ms, JIT {5} ms, waiting for a core {6} ms | marks: {7}
settings-showadvanced-hint: Shows every Komet switch. The hidden ones give the engine's own result, only faster or with less garbage, and stay on as they are; turn this on to look into one or switch it off while hunting a problem.
settings-rebuild-hint: Every chunk pool is freed (OpenGL's and Vulkan's video memory) and all loaded chunks are tessellated again into new pools, without leaving the world: switches such as compact terrain data or lean take effect at once. The terrain fills in again over a few seconds.
settings-hardware: This computer: {0} cores, {1} GB RAM, {2} GB video memory, {3} Hz
settings-detected-hint: Gives every option you changed on these pages back to the preset and to what suits this computer (chunk packing by RAM, pool trimming and distant foliage by video memory, the Vulkan far cache and frame bridge by video memory and monitor). The HUD and tool settings stay.
settings-exact-all: All exact optimisations of this page ({0})
settings-exact-all-hint: Every switch below at once. Each one gives exactly the game's own result, only faster or with less garbage; switch one off only to look for a fault, and tell which one in a bug report.
settings-preset-hint: Sets view distance, shadows, effects, particles and resolution in one go. Changing one of them afterwards makes the preset Custom.
settings-original-hint: Opens the game's own settings screen, as it looks without Komet.
settings-key-hint: Click, then press the key, key combination or mouse button to bind. Escape keeps the old one; a right click puts back the game's default.
settings-reset-hint: Click twice: the first click only asks.
settings-slider-keys: ← → one step · Shift: ten steps · Home / End · Delete: default · Tab: next slider
settings-graphicsmenu-hint: Shows this menu instead of the game's settings. Off: the game's own menu.
settings-menublur: Blur the game behind the menu
settings-menublur-hint: The world and the HUD behind this menu, blurred. Off: only darkened.
settings-held: Held at the game's own behaviour while another mod asks for it; your choice applies again once it lets go.
settings-shaderusecache-hint: Uploads only the shader uniforms that changed instead of all of them.
settings-distantshadows-hint: Terrain casts shadows up to the view distance, where the engine's shadows end after about 200 blocks. A third shadow map covers the far terrain; it is redrawn only when the sun has moved or you travelled far, a sixteenth per frame, so it costs little. Near shadows are the engine's.
settings-occlusionculling-hint: Leaves out terrain hidden behind other terrain, found on the GPU from the depth of what is already drawn. Two passes: what the last frame's depth hides is tested again against this frame's, so nothing shows a frame late. Runs only while Vulkan draws the opaque terrain ("Vulkan: opaque terrain"); in OpenGL the engine's own culling applies.
settings-gputerrainculling: Terrain culling fully on the GPU
settings-gputerrainculling-hint: With occlusion culling on: the GPU keeps every location of the opaque terrain's pools and tests them itself - the engine's visibility flags, the frustum, the LOD ranges and the depth pyramid - so the CPU no longer culls the opaque terrain's chunks nor gathers their boxes each frame. Needs doubles in compute shaders; without them the CPU culls as before. About 1.5 ms faster a frame on average, the 1 % lows equal to slightly lower.
settings-facesorting-hint: With the terrain culled fully on the GPU: the opaque and topsoil chunk meshes are sorted by the direction their faces face while they are built, and the GPU leaves out every direction facing away from the camera before a vertex is computed - about half of those faces. Faces the shader moves (wind, water) are always drawn. The picture stays the same.
settings-vulkan-advanced: Advanced: each part on its own
settings-vulkanonly-hint: Experimental. Vulkan draws everything in the world by itself and OpenGL rests: it keeps only the menu, the loading screens and the game's object names. Needs no OpenGL sharing extensions. Textures and buffers still reach OpenGL too, so on any error OpenGL takes over at once (the next frame is drawn by OpenGL; what only Vulkan drew, such as map tiles and icons, is written back to OpenGL first). With the lean switch, OpenGL gets no copy of the large ones and cannot take over. Whatever Vulkan cannot draw yet is missing from the picture; the log and the Vulkan report list what is missing. Best switched on before a world is joined.
settings-vulkanonlylean-hint: Experimental, with Vulkan only. OpenGL gets no copy of the world's large textures and buffers (atlases, shadow maps, screen targets, non-persistent chunk pools): saves the video memory of that second copy, typically several hundred MB. If Vulkan only is switched off or fails in a world, they are first given back to OpenGL from Vulkan's (a short pause); only after a GPU fault does OpenGL show just the menus over a black frame, and the world must be left and joined again. Takes effect for what a world loads after it is switched on, so best switched on before joining.
settings-vulkanframebridge-hint: Experimental, with Vulkan only and Vulkan showing the frames. When the game misses a refresh of the monitor (a garbage collection, a spike, or simply a monitor faster than the frames), Komet shows the last frame turned to where the camera is going, continued from the last two frames' turn. Turning stays smooth at the monitor's refresh rate; the GUI and the first-person hand stay as the game drew them. Moving entities and walking show only at the game's own frame rate. Costs two screen-sized copies a frame on the GPU.
settings-vulkanfarcache: Vulkan only: cache the far terrain (experimental)
settings-vulkanfarcache-hint: Experimental, with Vulkan only and GPU terrain culling, from a view distance of 448 blocks. The terrain past 384 blocks is drawn into a layer of its own only every 12th frame (or after a step of a block or a new field of view) and laid into the frames in between, turned to where the camera looks. Far terrain that comes into view when turning is drawn at once. Saves most of the far terrain's GPU time at large view distances; costs one screen-sized layer of video memory.
settings-vulkanquietuniforms: Vulkan only: uniforms kept from resting OpenGL
settings-vulkanquietuniforms-hint: With Vulkan only, the shader values the game sets every frame are kept by Komet instead of being sent to the idle OpenGL as well; OpenGL gets them all at once should it draw again (Vulkan only switched off or failing). Saves about 0.15 ms of the main thread per frame.
settings-vulkan-mode-hint: OpenGL: the game's own renderer. Vulkan (experimental): Vulkan draws the whole world, the window and the GUI alone and OpenGL rests; what Vulkan cannot draw is missing from the picture, and on any error OpenGL draws everything again. Takes effect on the next frame.
settings-vulkanpacing-hint: Waits for the GPU at the very start of a frame, before the game reads its clock, instead of in the middle of the frame. When the GPU is the limit, frames then start (and the camera moves) at the same even pace the GPU finishes and shows them, instead of jittering with the CPU's work before the wait.
settings-vulkangputimes-hint: Times the GPU's work in the Vulkan frame with timestamps - per render stage and what is drawn (terrain, sky, entities, particles, post-processing, compute) - and writes the milliseconds per frame into the report in the log. Costs a few dozen timestamps a frame.
settings-vulkanshadercache-hint: Keeps the game's shaders as Vulkan translated them (SPIR-V), the uniforms found to change with every draw, and the driver's pipeline cache on disk (VintagestoryData/Cache/komet-vulkan), for this computer and GPU. At the next start a shader seen before is read back instead of translated and compiled again on the render thread, which takes away most of the stutter when the world, a creature or a particle first shows up. A new Komet version translates anew.
settings-vulkancompactfaces-hint: With Vulkan only, the terrain's face data is kept in 52 bytes a quad instead of 64 (the edges as half floats; corner, textures, flags and colours unchanged): about 15 % less video memory for the terrain, some 0.6 GB at view distance 1536. Packed as each chunk is uploaded and unpacked by the shaders; exact for blocks on the 1/16 grid, within 1/2000 of an edge for turned models. Switching it rebuilds the terrain at once (in a few seconds, without leaving the world).
settings-frustumsweep-hint: Culls chunk meshes with vector instructions and a grid, with the engine's result and order. From 8,192 entries per pass the worker threads help.
settings-leanvaryings-hint: The terrain's vertex shaders hand fewer values to the fragment shaders: what follows from the block's flags, the uniforms or the world position (normal, glow, fog colour, camera position, the shadow maps' coordinates) is worked out per pixel instead. The same picture up to the last bit of rounding. Takes effect when the shaders load next.
settings-ssaolean-hint: At the high SSAO quality: 16 sample points a pixel instead of 24 and one blur pass instead of three, as at medium quality. The ambient occlusion looks a little softer and noisier; about 0.1-0.3 ms a frame at 1080p, more at higher resolutions.
settings-nearshadowreuse: Reuse the near shadow map between frames
settings-nearshadowreuse-hint: The near shadow map (the 30 to 40 blocks around you, 1.5 ms of GPU a frame in a forest) is drawn once and kept for up to 17 ms while the sun, the terrain in it and your position stay, and your view turns less than about two degrees; the map is drawn two blocks wider for that, a twentieth less shadow resolution. Below 60 fps every frame draws it, so nothing lags. Off: as the game, every frame.
settings-farshadowreuse-hint: The far shadow map is kept for up to 33 ms instead of being redrawn every frame: the sun moves a few thousandths of a degree in that time and the map follows the camera exactly. Redrawn at once when terrain in its range changes, the light turns or the camera jumps. Entity shadows beyond the near map update at about 30 Hz.
settings-farfoliage-hint: Past the distance where one block covers less than this many pixels (from the window height, the resolution and the field of view), every other leaf block is left out in a checkerboard (each leaf block is two crossed quads two blocks wide, so its neighbours cover the gap) and grass, flowers, ferns and crops are left out. At 1 pixel the difference is hardly visible; distant forests draw about half the triangles. Chunks crossing the line are retessellated as you move. 0 turns it off.
settings-deepculling-hint: Chunks whose top lies 16 blocks below the surface of all their neighbouring columns (sea floors and pits count as surface) hold cave walls nobody sees from above, about a fifth to a third of all terrain at a large view distance. Farther than 96 blocks from you (256 when you are under the surface: in a cave, mine or house) they are kept without geometry, which saves video memory; coming near brings them back.
settings-leangodrays-hint: The god rays read the scene's colour only where it adds to them (the sky), not behind the terrain: the same picture, fewer texture reads.
settings-framepacer-hint: Waits for the fps cap's exact interval instead of whole milliseconds as the game does, which makes capped frames alternate between short and long (microstutter) and overshoots the cap. Only with VSync off and an fps cap set.
settings-sharpupscale-hint: Below 100 % resolution the scene is upscaled to the window as AMD FSR 1 does (edge-aware, twelve texels) instead of stretched with one bilinear sample: edges stay sharp. At 100 % nothing changes.
settings-entitycasters: Entity shadows culled by the view
settings-entitycasters-hint: Like the shadow casters of the terrain: creatures, players and dropped items whose shadow, cast along the light, cannot reach your view (with 8 blocks to spare) are left out of the shadow maps. The shadows on screen stay the same.
settings-indirectdraw-hint: Draws chunk batches as indirect commands from a mapped GPU buffer. Needs GL_ARB_multi_draw_indirect; without it the engine draws.
settings-sunocclusion-hint: Reads the sun's occlusion query every fourth frame instead of every frame; under Mesa every glGet is a sync.
settings-windowsizecache-hint: Remembers the window size the engine asks GLFW for a dozen times per frame (on X11 a round trip to the display server).
settings-poolscale-hint: A chunk render pass's second mesh pool is twice the configured size and every later one this many times: the same meshes in fewer pools, so fewer draw calls and culling jobs. Passes with little in them keep their size. Applies to pools made from now on, fully after rejoining; 1 is the engine.
settings-pooltrim-hint: The game never gives a chunk pool back, so flying across the map leaves gigabytes of mostly empty pools in video memory. 1: a pool without a chunk for 10 s is freed. 2: after 2 s, and the sparsest old pool of a pass (under 25 % used) is drained: it takes no new chunks and its chunks are tessellated again into the others, a few dozen a second, until it is empty and freed. 3: after 1 s, pools under 50 % used, twice as fast. 4: pools under 75 % used, four times as fast; 5: under 90 %, eight times as fast (more retessellation in the background). 0: off.
settings-chunkpacking-hint: The game packs a chunk's block and light data only after 8 s untouched and at most 50 chunks a second, so flying leaves thousands unpacked in RAM. 1: 200 a second; 2: 400 a second, after half the time; 3: 800 a second, after a quarter, and at most 500 spare chunk datas kept (the game keeps up to 4000). More CPU on a background thread while flying, less RAM. 0: the game's own.
settings-recyclertrim-hint: The game keeps meshes the tessellation gave back for reuse, up to some 3.4 million quads (about 200-500 MB), and lets go of one at a time. 1: half of that, dropped after 8 s unused; 2: a quarter, after 4 s, and chiselled blocks farther than 6 chunks drop their mesh once it is in the chunk (made again when the chunk is next tessellated). Also gives the tesselators' scratch meshes, grown to the largest chunk, back once nothing waited for tessellation for 10 s. Fewer kept meshes, slightly more allocation while chunks load. 0: the game's own.
settings-glerrorpoll-hint: The two error checks the engine makes every frame ask the driver only every 16th time. Under Mesa's glthread each check makes the main thread wait for the driver thread; no error is lost, it is only logged a few frames later. Off while the GL debug mode is on.
settings-chunklookup-hint: Answers chunk lookups from a mirror instead of under the lock every client thread takes.
settings-animationframes-hint: Takes animation frames from a cache, otherwise compiles them quickly, otherwise leaves them to the engine.
settings-initonce-hint: Leaves out the second, identical init of the player's shape on every re-tessellation.
settings-shapeinitmemo-hint: Skips repeated inits of entity shapes that did not change.
settings-meshpool-hint: Inserts and removes chunk meshes without walking every pool entry, bit-identical to the engine.
settings-meshrecycle-hint: Recycled meshes keep the arrays the engine allocates anew for every clone.
settings-facepacking-hint: Packs the faces of a chunk upload on Komet's worker threads instead of one after the other on the main thread.

hud-rendercost: Terrain draw cost per frame, main thread
hud-rc-nothreads: No Mesa driver threads found (Linux with Mesa only)

hud-occ-drawn-late: Ranges drawn in the second pass
hud-pipeline: Opaque terrain in the GPU pipeline (one frame)

hud-glerror-skipped: GL error checks left out per frame
hud-debug-timings: Debug build – Komet's own timings are inflated roughly 2.6x
hud-cull-sorted: Pools sorted into the grid per frame
hud-cull-staged: Render calls culled with their stage
hud-anim-idle: Idle animation calls left out per frame
hud-draw-unmapped: GL_ARB_buffer_storage missing, command buffer per draw
hud-anim-fast-blocked: Another mod patches the compile, or the game changed it: engine path
hud-pool-trimmed-mb: Video memory freed from empty pools
hud-entitytess-unpatched: Budget {0} ms - substitution failed, every entity tessellates at once
hud-entitytess-deferred: Put off to a later frame
hud-entitytimes-unpatched: The entity loops are not the ones measured: no times
hud-shapememo-blocked: Another mod patches the shape init, or the game changed it: engine path
hud-particlelight-unpatched: Patch not installed, particles wait as in the engine
hud-particlelight-reads: Light reads on the render thread per frame
hud-particlelight-packed: Chunk packed, not unpacked per frame
hud-extendedrows-unpatched: Rewrite did not match the game's code, the engine copies cell by cell (see log)
hud-extendedrows-blocked: Another mod patches the chunk reads, the engine copies cell by cell
hud-extendedrows-fallbacks: Handed to the engine per frame
hud-visiblefaces-unpatched: Patch not installed, the engine computes every chunk
hud-visiblefaces-other: Another patch on the method, the engine computes every chunk
hud-visiblefaces-engine: Chunks left to the engine (unknown cull mode)
hud-visiblefaces-ported: Cells by the engine's logic (special cull mode, snow)
hud-owntess-unpatched: Not installed, the engine draws every block
hud-owntess-other: Another patch on a tessellator body, the engine draws the blocks it concerns
hud-owntess-json: Of these, simple models per frame
hud-facelight-unpatched: Patch not installed, the engine lights every face
hud-facelight-other: Another patch on the face light, the engine lights the faces it concerns
hud-facelight-blocks: JSON blocks lit in one pass per frame
hud-tess-unpatched: Counters not installed, tessellation is not measured
hud-tess-partial: A fast path did not match the game's code, the engine's version runs (see log)
hud-tess-occluded-other: Another patch on the tessellation, enclosed chunks go to the engine
hud-tess-zero: Time in chunks without a vertex
hud-tess-skipped: Empty or missing chunks per second
hud-farfoliage-unpatched: The tessellator changed, foliage is drawn in full at every distance
hud-farfoliage-thinned: Leaf blocks thinned out per second
hud-farfoliage-marked: Chunks retessellated for distance per second
hud-tess-workers-failed: Tessellation on a worker thread failed, the engine tessellates alone again (see log)
hud-tess-workers-unpatched: No tessellation on the worker threads: not every safety patch is installed
settings-entitytessbudget-hint: Milliseconds per frame for re-tessellating entities; the rest waits for the next frame. 0 = the engine, all at once.
settings-partitionreuse-hint: Reuses the grid EntityPartitioning rebuilds 31 times a second, on the client and the singleplayer server, instead of allocating it anew. Removes about 7 MB/s of garbage in a large world.
settings-cookingmatch-hint: A firepit with a cooking pot asks every cooking recipe twice a second whether the contents match, and each ask copied the stacks, the ingredients and the ignored attributes. The checks now reuse their lists. Same result as the engine.
settings-handlerlists-hint: Every climate and wind lookup copied the list of its event's handlers into a new array. The list is now made again only when a handler is added or removed. Particles also keep their block walk callback, and the room registry its scratch set for changed blocks, instead of making new ones on every call. Same result as the engine.
settings-animatableculling-hint: Skips the draw of an animated block entity (doors, chests, translocators, machinery in ruins) whose model lies wholly outside the view or the shadow map. The engine draws every one in three passes each frame, however far away.
settings-helpcompose: Block interaction help composed only on change
settings-helpcompose-hint: The game draws the interaction help (the keys and items shown at a block or creature) anew at every block looked at, every third of a second at a creature and at every block change nearby, 5 to 15 ms of the main thread each time, even when the lines would be the same. Komet skips the redraw while the actions, keys and items shown stay the same.
settings-potculling: Pots on firepits in view only
settings-potculling-hint: A pot on a firepit draws itself and its lid every frame wherever it stands, even behind the camera. With this on, a pot wholly outside the view is left out; one that could show a pixel of itself is drawn as before.
settings-glquerycache-hint: The game's cloud renderer asks the graphics driver for the current framebuffer and viewport every frame. With a threaded driver each question waits until the driver's thread has caught up. With this on Komet answers them from what it saw being set. Same values as the driver.
settings-protolistcache-hint: Every received chunk carries a dictionary of mod data, and the serializer looked up by reflection, each time anew, how to fill that kind of collection. With this on the answer is looked up once per kind. Same data as the engine.
settings-bushshapes-hint: Each new look of a berry bush (health, berry stage, texture) parsed the bush's shape file again before building its mesh: hundreds of times in a world full of bushes. With this on each shape file is parsed once. Same meshes as the engine.
settings-cluttermeshes-hint: Every decor block entity the world generator places (pots, crates, books, bones, rubble) kept its own rotated copy of its block's mesh for as long as it lived, though the copy is only read while its chunk is tessellated: the largest share of memory the garbage collector promoted while chunks load, apart from the chunks themselves. With this on the copy is built for each tessellation and dropped afterwards. Same meshes as the engine.
settings-cullerrays-hint: The engine's occlusion culling casts thousands of rays through the chunk grid on its own thread and tested all six faces of every cell through vector objects: about a tenth of all the work the game did while a world loaded, a core taken from chunk tessellation. With this on the same rays are walked on plain numbers, testing only the faces a ray can leave through. Same visible chunks as the engine.
settings-mapreads: World map reads one lock per chunk
settings-mapreads-hint: The world map read each column's surface block on its own, taking the chunk's lock for every one of a map piece's thousand reads, against the tessellation threads that hold the same locks: the most contended thread while a world loads. With this on each chunk is locked once per map piece and its blocks read together. Same map as the engine.
settings-ascii85text-hint: When the world generator places a rotated structure, each of its block entities is encoded to text with a new five-character buffer for every four bytes: the integrated server's largest source of garbage while new land generates, and its garbage triggers the game's collections too. With this on the text is written in one piece. Same text as the engine.
settings-treekeys: Block entity data without key copies
settings-treekeys-hint: Every block entity arriving with a chunk had each of its attribute names read into a new string only to be swapped for the shared one at once. With this on the shared name is looked up straight from the received bytes. Same data as the engine.
settings-mappixels-hint: Every piece of the world map was drawn into a new array that waited for its save and its upload and so survived a garbage collection: the largest single share of what the collections copied while exploring. With this on the arrays are reused once both are done. Same map as the engine.
settings-mapsavescratch-hint: The world map stores every map piece it draws in its database, serializing each into a growing buffer first: while chunks stream in, about 40 MB of garbage a second, and the collections it causes stop the game. With this on the same rows are written from one reused buffer. Same data as the engine.
settings-maptileupload: Map tiles without a framebuffer per piece
settings-maptileupload-hint: Every new piece of the world map is drawn into its map tile through a framebuffer of its own, which switches the whole render target twice per piece: while chunks stream in, up to 200 pieces per game tick and stutters on the render thread. With this on, each piece is uploaded straight into its tile. Same image as the engine.
settings-maptileculling-hint: A map, the minimap included, draws every map tile the game holds each frame, up to a thousand at a large view distance, though only a dozen show. With this on, a tile wholly outside the map is left out. Under Vulkan each drawn tile needs a copy of its own, which made joining a world stutter for many seconds.
settings-idleanimators-hint: Block entities that can animate (chests, doors, querns...) have the engine call their animation and their renderer every frame, animating or not. A call that would return without doing anything is left out. Same result as the engine.
settings-tessblockpos-hint: The tesselator no longer allocates a new position for every plant and crop it asks how far to lower itself. Only for blocks whose code is proven not to keep it.
settings-climatecache-hint: Keeps every climate region in view (up to 144) instead of a fixed 10 regions of 1 MiB each.
hud-prejit-cancelled: Cancelled - world left or switched off
hud-prejit-idle: Not started - switched off at world join
settings-prejit-hint: At world join, on a background thread: fewer JIT stalls the first time something runs.
settings-decompressscratch-hint: Unpacks chunk layers without a throwaway copy: about 8 MB/s less garbage while chunks arrive.
settings-columnnoisescratch-hint: Computes terrain noise with reused arrays. Singleplayer world generation only.
settings-extendedrows-hint: Copies a chunk and its neighbours for the tesselator 32 cells at a time instead of cell by cell.
settings-visiblefaces-hint: Finds visible block faces with a bit formula instead of a case per face.
settings-facelight-hint: Computes block face light (smooth shadows) from bits, four corners at once, without virtual calls.
settings-lightscratch-hint: Spreads block light with reused objects instead of throwaway ones.
settings-lightrepair-hint: The engine's relight (WorldEdit, /debug relight, the timeswitch) leaves chunks of columns not loaded whole without any light, drawn black, and puts light sources in the wrong place. Komet relights without these faults, lights such chunks when they load and checks the loaded columns every 200 ms; the repair is saved. Singleplayer only.
settings-particlelight-hint: Particles take the chunk lock only when it is free, otherwise the light read last. Removes long 8-13 ms frames near beehives.
settings-occludedchunks-hint: A chunk enclosed on all sides by opaque blocks yields no vertices and is not tessellated.
settings-tessschedule-hint: Tessellates the nearest chunk first, weighted by view direction, instead of in arrival order. Nearby chunks wait half as long.
settings-workerthreads-hint: Threads for culling and tessellation, at most. How many of them work at any moment Komet decides by itself (see the priority). 0 = only the game's own threads.
settings-tesspriority-hint: What Komet's worker threads spend themselves on. 0 % = no tessellation on them, the game's own thread loads chunks alone: the smoothest frames. Low values: a few threads, and fewer as soon as the main thread has to wait for a CPU core. 100 % = every worker thread, chunks load as fast as possible, the main thread is given way only late. How many threads work right now Komet decides by itself; a large backlog (joining a world, teleporting) lifts the share.
hud-garbage-unpatched: A rewrite did not match the game's code, the engine's version runs (see log)
hud-garbage-decompress: Chunk layer copies saved per frame
hud-garbage-noise: Terrain noise arrays saved per frame
settings-uploadcap-hint: Milliseconds per frame for uploading chunks and the pool work they cause; priority chunks go first, up to their ceiling of 6 ms. 0 = the engine's own budget, no cap.
settings-uploadyield-hint: A frame that is already slow when its chunk uploads come (a garbage collection or a burst of block entities before them, 6 ms past the usual) uploads only one chunk and leaves the rest to the next frame, never two frames in a row. Chunks next to you and block edits still go at once. Shortens the worst frames; the world fills in a frame later at most.
hud-uploadcap-active: Upload time cap: {0} ms per frame
hud-uploadcap-off: Upload time cap off, engine budget only
hud-uploadcap-unpatched: Upload time cap {0} ms - substitution failed, engine budget only
hud-upload-over: Frames whose chunk work went past the cap
hud-upload-over-ms: Past the cap by, per such frame
hud-upload-priority-cut: Frames that left priority chunks for the next
hud-upload-births: Chunk pools adopted as made, per second
settings-chunkloadbudget-hint: Milliseconds per frame for setting up arriving chunks and their block entities and for unloading old ones. Chunks more than three columns away wait for the next frame, in arrival order; nearby chunks always go at once. 0 = the engine, all at once.
settings-eventbussweep-hint: Ground storage, shelves, racks and firepits never removed their event listener, so every one ever loaded stayed in memory and each new one took longer to set up. Unloaded and broken ones are now released. Same behaviour as the engine.
hud-chunkload-unpatched: Chunk arrival budget: substitution failed, the engine loads all at once
cmd-debug: records everything Komet measures and writes the debug protocol: [seconds|now|spike <ms>|stop] [en|de]
cmd-debug-usage: Usage: /komet debug [seconds | now | spike <ms> | stop] [en | de]
cmd-debug-running: A debug capture is already running or being written.
cmd-debug-bench: The HUD benchmark is running; start the capture after it.
cmd-debug-started: Debug capture running for {0} s, every collector on.

settings-gclatency-hint: The garbage collector may no longer stop the game to compact the whole heap: with a large view distance that stop took seconds. Full collections run alongside the game instead; only when memory runs short does the runtime still stop. Same game behaviour, a little more memory.
settings-gccompact-hint: With the low-latency collector the game's memory freed in the middle of the heap (packed chunks, freed pools) stays reserved, often gigabytes. When the game is paused or its window has been out of focus for 10 s and over 1 GB lies fragmented, the heap is compacted once and the memory given back to the system (a pause of a few seconds nobody sees), at most every 2 minutes.

settings-inventoryshapes-hint: Creature items and clothing build their inventory mesh from shape files that also hold every animation: the first look at a row of them in the creative inventory froze the game for up to two seconds. Komet reads these shapes without the animations, which the mesh never uses. The icons look the same.
settings-selectionscratch-hint: The ray that finds the block you look at asks every block it steps over for decor selection boxes, and the game makes a new list for each, nearly always empty: 4 % of all allocations. Komet hands it one list per thread, cleared each time.
settings-profilerpool-hint: The game's frame profiler, which Komet's HUD switches on for its render-pass rows, makes a dictionary and an entry per mark anew every frame: 12 % of all allocations in a steady-state trace. Komet keeps two sets of them and zeroes them as the frame begins; a mark allocates only the first time its code is seen.
settings-patchlookup: Vegetation patches without a mod lookup
settings-patchlookup-hint: Every vegetation patch the world generates asks the mod loader for a mod system and drops the answer, a walk over every mod system with an iterator and a closure each time (2 % of all allocations while terrain streams in). Komet answers without looking.
settings-iconbudget: Spread new inventory icons over frames
settings-iconbudget-hint: Many items build their icon mesh the first time they are shown, 5 to 15 ms each: a new row of the creative inventory took 150 ms. Komet draws such first-time icons for at most 6 ms a frame; the rest appear a few frames later. Icons already drawn once are never held back.
settings-worldgenscratch-hint: In singleplayer the world generator shares the game's memory and garbage collection pauses. The sunlight flood, the rock strata, the plant patches and the chunk request queue reuse what they used to allocate anew for every position, column, block and tick: about 1 GB a minute less while flying into new terrain. The world comes out the same.
settings-serverprocess: Experimental: singleplayer server in its own process
settings-serverprocess-hint: Experimental. Starts a singleplayer world's server as a process of its own (the game's server program) and connects to it locally. Only the client stays in the game's memory; world generation and server logic run apart: flying into new terrain and landing there, allocation halves (80 → 33 MB/s) and GC pauses fall from 7.6 % to 3.1 % of the time (bench). Costs about 3 GB of RAM more and about 15 s longer loading; mods expecting client and server in one process may break. Worth it from 24 GB of RAM.
host-handover: Komet: moving the world's server into its own process...
host-previous: Komet: waiting for the previous server to finish saving...
settings-jitwarm: Tessellation code optimized from the start
settings-jitwarm-hint: The engine's large tessellation methods are compiled optimized at their first call. Left alone, .NET runs them unoptimized for the first seconds of a world, while thousands of new methods are compiled, and every chunk takes 10 to 20 times as long: the terrain comes in later. Takes effect from the next world start. The meshes come out the same.
settings-blockentitybudget: Far block entities spread over frames
settings-blockentitybudget-hint: A chunk more than three columns away sets up its block entities (firepits, ground storage, racks and the like) one by one within the chunk arrival budget, and goes on next frame where it stopped. The chunk shows up once all of them are done, and nothing queued behind it overtakes it; nearby chunks still come in one go. Each block entity is set up once, in the engine's order, and one that something reads before its turn is set up right then. Works with the chunk arrival budget.
settings-blockentitycaches-hint: Ground storage parsed its whole storage settings as JSON to read one number, firepits rebuilt their mesh at every redraw (the engine never kept it) and parsed the pot and lid shapes for every pot on the fire at every update. Each of these is now worked out once per kind and reused. Same results as the engine.
settings-listenerslots-hint: Every block entity that loads registers tick listeners, renderers and event listeners, and the engine searched its whole list of them from the start each time: the longer the session, the slower every chunk. The place is now found without the search. Same lists in the same order as the engine.
settings-owntessellation: Own tessellator for cubes, soil and simple models
settings-owntessellation-hint: Komet's own tessellator draws cube blocks, layers, grassy soil and simple model blocks such as sand, gravel and loose stones: each face written straight into the chunk mesh, its texture and light chosen as the engine chooses them, with code optimized from a world's first second. Blocks with their own drawing code (plants, leaves, block entities, mods) and any block it does not cover exactly, the engine draws as before. The meshes come out the same.
settings-partrecycling-hint: Small chunk meshes come from the engine's mesh recycler like large ones and go back to it after their upload, and the tessellation threads and the upload reuse their decor table, ocean corners and location lists instead of making new ones for every chunk. The meshes come out the same.
